title: Market income, transfers and taxes tell different stories about household security
source_unit: Congressional Budget Office, The Distribution of Household Income, 2023, September 2026
geography: United States; approximately 134 million households, income quintiles and top 1 percent, 1979–2023

observations.period: 2023; household income before and after means-tested transfers and federal taxes

total_income.unit: approximately trillion dollars in household income

bottom_quintile_before_transfers_taxes.unit: percent change in average income before transfers and taxes from 2022 to 2023, inflation-adjusted

top_one_percent_before_transfers_taxes.unit: percent change in average income before transfers and taxes from 2022 to 2023, inflation-adjusted

after_transfers_taxes.value: income was more equally distributed after transfers and taxes than before them; in 2023 average income after transfers and taxes rose 4% for the lowest quintile and fell 5% for the highest quintile

mechanism.value: Household security depends on the interaction of earnings, capital income, transfers and taxes rather than on market income alone

observations.method: CBO distributional analysis using tax-return data, survey data and administrative information to estimate income before and after means-tested transfers and federal taxes; all dollar amounts are inflation-adjusted to 2023 dollars.
observations.uncertainty: The report estimates average group outcomes and does not identify within-quintile variation, individual transitions, material consumption, wealth, debt, regional costs or causal effects of any single transfer or tax policy.
observations.subgroup: U.S. households in five income quintiles and the top 1 percent, including households whose income includes labor, business, capital, social-insurance and means-tested-transfer components.
observations.counterinterpretation: A one-year decline at the top driven largely by realized capital gains may not indicate lasting deterioration; average quintile changes can conceal substantial heterogeneity and household mobility.

observations.period: 2022–2023; means-tested transfers and federal taxes at the bottom of the distribution

means_tested_transfer_rate.unit: percentage-point change in means-tested transfers as a share of income before transfers and taxes for the lowest quintile

federal_tax_rate.unit: percentage-point change in the federal tax rate for the lowest quintile

offset.value: the 1 percentage-point decrease in the federal tax rate partially offset the 2 percentage-point decrease in means-tested transfers

inequality_effect.value: transfers and taxes made household income more equally distributed, while the extent of their inequality reduction was similar in 2023 and 2022

mechanism.value: The same household can experience income security through a changing package of market earnings, public transfers and tax liability; policy withdrawal and tax changes are not interchangeable forms of relief

observations.method: CBO comparison of income before transfers and taxes, means-tested transfer rates, federal tax rates and income after transfers and taxes by income group.
observations.uncertainty: Average transfer and tax rates do not measure eligibility take-up, benefit adequacy, administrative access, service use, tax incidence across households or the reasons for year-over-year changes.
observations.subgroup: Lower-income households receiving or eligible for Medicaid, CHIP, SNAP, SSI and other means-tested assistance, as well as households affected by federal income, payroll, corporate and excise taxes.
observations.counterinterpretation: A lower transfer rate can reflect changing income, eligibility, program rules or utilization rather than a simple withdrawal of support; lower tax rates can coexist with reduced public benefits or higher nonfederal costs.

observations.period: 1979–2023; long-run income growth, inequality and redistribution

denominator.unit: CBO long-run household income distribution series

lowest_quintile_average_income.value: average annual income rose from $19,000 in 1979 to $28,500 in 2023, in 2023 dollars

highest_quintile_average_income.value: average annual income rose from $179,700 in 1979 to $409,300 in 2023, in 2023 dollars

inequality.value: income inequality rose from 1979 to 2023 both before and after transfers and taxes

redistribution.value: the degree to which transfers and taxes reduced inequality increased over time, with means-tested transfers growing especially for the lowest quintile and driven primarily by Medicaid spending

mechanism.value: Long-run income growth can coexist with widening relative distance, making public redistribution part of the social contract that determines whether growth is experienced as shared security

observations.method: CBO historical distributional series from 1979 through 2023, separating market and social-insurance income, means-tested transfers, federal taxes and income after transfers and taxes.
observations.uncertainty: The long-run series are average group estimates and do not establish intergenerational mobility, lifetime income, household wealth, consumption, health, political response or the causal effect of Medicaid or other programs.
observations.subgroup: Households across the income distribution, workers, beneficiaries of social insurance and means-tested programs, taxpayers, and communities evaluating whether economic growth is broadly shared.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rising inequality measures do not by themselves establish declining absolute welfare; the lowest quintile experienced real average income growth, and transfers and taxes can reduce inequality without eliminating other forms of insecurity.

boundary: This record identifies a U.S. distributional, transfer-tax, household-security and fiscal-legitimacy subtheme. It does not establish individual mobility, consumption, wealth, debt, material hardship, benefit adequacy, administrative access, political response or the causal effect of a specific tax or transfer; those require linked household, program, state, service and political episodes.
